We tend to hold that people deserve praise or blame only for what lies within their control. A man cannot be blamed for his height, nor credited with the fortunate accident of his birth, and a principle seems to follow: moral assessment must track the will and not the outcome. Kant gave the principle its most austere expression when he said that a good will shines like a jewel by its own light, whatever it achieves or fails to achieve. Nor can we escape by appeal to intention alone, since intentions are themselves shaped by character. Yet a moment's reflection on ordinary judgement suggests that we do not apply the principle consistently. We treat a driver who kills a child running into the road quite differently from one who, driving in exactly the same way, merely reached home, and we treat an attempted murder differently from a murder that succeeded, though the difference between them may be a gust of wind that deflected a bullet.

In 1976 Thomas Nagel and Bernard Williams, in a famous exchange, gave the name moral luck to this predicament: people are morally assessed for features of their conduct that depend on factors beyond their control. Nagel distinguished several kinds. Resultant luck concerns how things turn out. Circumstantial luck concerns the situations in which one is placed, as when a man who might have collaborated under a tyranny lives out his life in a peaceful country and escapes the test. Constitutive luck concerns the temperament with which one is born, and causal luck the extent to which one's actions are determined by antecedent circumstances. The point is that the principle that we are responsible only for what we control, when pressed, seems to dissolve nearly everything we hold people responsible for, since almost nothing, the will itself included, is wholly under control. Moral luck is a problem, in short, not about exotic cases but about the fabric of ordinary responsibility.

Williams approached the problem through the imagined case of a painter modelled on Gauguin, who abandons his family to paint in Tahiti. Whether his decision was justified, Williams argued, depends on whether he turns out to be a great painter, which he could not know when he decided. If he fails, we say he was wrong; if he succeeds, his choice is vindicated, and not merely excused. The justification is retrospective and therefore hostage to luck. Yet Williams did not conclude that the judgement is mistaken. He insisted that it reflects something true about our moral relation to our own lives: a driver who looks back on a terrible act that he did not intend feels a regret that differs in kind from the regret of a bystander, and to lose this feeling would be to lose part of what it is to be an agent. Williams called it agent-regret.

Defenders of the control principle reply that the apparent role of luck is an illusion produced by confusing different judgements. We may regret an outcome and pity the person to whom it happened, they say, without blaming him: the unlucky driver deserves sympathy, not condemnation. What differs between the two drivers is how we feel, not what each deserves. The reply has force, but it carries a cost. If outcomes do not affect desert at all, then the law's gradation of penalties by result, with heavier punishment for the successful murderer than for the unsuccessful one, is unjust, and so, many would add, is the ordinary practice of holding people to account for the consequences of their negligence.

A subtler response distinguishes between what a person is answerable for and what he is blameworthy for. A person who takes on a risk, such as driving, takes on a responsibility for how it turns out; if harm results, he owes an apology and compensation, whatever care he took. This is a liability that does not depend on fault, and it is familiar from law: a landowner may be liable for damage done by a wild animal he kept, though he took every precaution. The proposal preserves the control principle for blame while acknowledging that morality assigns burdens by outcome. But critics note that the distinction is unstable. If answerability involves real moral demands, such as the duty to make amends, then outcomes do matter morally, and the control principle has been given up at one level in order to be retained at another.

The debate has a practical edge. Consider how we judge historical figures, our parents, or ourselves. People who lived ordinary lives under regimes that made moral heroism very costly are praised or blamed for what they would have done in circumstances that never arose, and we usually refrain from condemning those who were never tested. This restraint is a recognition of circumstantial luck; it suggests that we already believe character to be partly a matter of fortune. But the restraint cuts both ways. If the untested are spared condemnation because they were lucky, then the heroes who were tested and passed might have failed in different circumstances, and their praise is likewise partly a matter of luck. Parents who raise children well in comfortable circumstances, and those who fail in desperate ones, are judged in much the same fashion, with little attention to the difficulty of the task.

What survives of the control principle, then, is less a rule than an ideal, one that shapes our reactions without governing them entirely. We keep the thought that persons deserve moral credit for what is up to them, and we find it hard to say what that is, since the boundary between an agent and the circumstances that formed her is not sharp. questions.question: Which of the following best captures the passage's overall position?
options: A) People are held responsible only for what they control, yet ordinary judgement departs from this, and no response fully reconciles the two.
B) Moral luck shows that the control principle is false, and that people ought to be judged entirely by the outcomes of what they do and by nothing else.
C) Williams demonstrated that agent-regret has no place in morality, because the regret of an agent is no different in kind from that of a bystander.
D) The control principle can be rescued by distinguishing blame from sympathy, and the debate over moral luck may therefore be regarded as settled.

options: A) constitutive luck, since Gauguin's gifts as a painter were fixed by the temperament with which he was born.

questions.question: Williams's notion of agent-regret implies that
options: A) every agent is blameworthy for harm he causes, however carefully he has acted in the circumstances.
B) regret is appropriate only for outcomes that the agent could have foreseen and could have prevented.

If speakers of different languages divide the spectrum in constrained ways, language could hardly be the shaper of colour perception.

Later work showed that the story was incomplete. In an experiment published in 2007, researchers examined Russian, which has separate basic terms for lighter and darker blues, goluboy and siniy, where English has one. Russian speakers were faster to discriminate two shades of blue when they fell on opposite sides of the boundary between those terms than when they fell on the same side; English speakers showed no such advantage. Crucially, the effect disappeared when participants performed a verbal task, such as holding a string of digits in memory, while discriminating the colours, but not when they performed a spatial task of comparable difficulty. The pattern suggests that the boundary matters, but through the language system itself, which is engaged in the discrimination unless it is occupied elsewhere. The effect is real; it is also small, fast and fragile.

Evidence of this kind has accumulated beyond colour. Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr, an Australian language that uses compass directions in place of left and right, are reported to keep track of their orientation with remarkable accuracy, even in unfamiliar surroundings, and to describe the layout of objects in cardinal terms that English speakers would find baffling. Studies of languages with grammatical gender have suggested that speakers' descriptions of objects may be coloured, however faintly, by the gender their language assigns to them. Studies of how speakers describe accidents, for example whether they name the agent of an accidental act, have also found differences in what witnesses later remember, though here again the effects are small. In such cases the claim is not that language makes some thoughts impossible but that it makes some thoughts habitual, because one cannot speak the language without attending to certain distinctions. As the linguist Roman Jakobson is usually paraphrased, languages differ essentially in what they must convey and not in what they may convey.

These findings should be handled with care, for the methodological problems are formidable. Correlations between language and cognition may arise because both reflect a culture, not because language shapes thought: a society that crosses open desert may develop both a vocabulary of compass directions and a skill at dead reckoning, and neither need cause the other. Experiments that compare two language groups also compare two populations that differ in education, habits and expectations, and a difference of a few hundredths of a second in a laboratory task may have many causes. Several celebrated results have proved difficult to replicate, and even those that survive tend to show effects that are modest and dependent on context. Small samples compound these difficulties. A sceptic may fairly say that the demonstrated influence of language on thought amounts to little.

The sceptic is right about the size of the effects and wrong about their significance. If language had no influence on thought, the hypothesis would be false; that it has some, even a modest one, shows that language is not a transparent window on a world of ready-made concepts but a practice that trains attention. What is at stake is therefore less whether language shapes thought than how, how much, and under what conditions. The question has become an empirical one, and its answers are likely to be a patchwork: strong in some domains and negligible in others, depending on how much a task draws on the language system. The practical lesson for readers of such studies is to ask of each result what, exactly, was varied, and whether the same effect would survive a change of task, population or time.
questions.question: The author's stance towards the sceptic in the last paragraph is best described as
options: A) complete agreement: the effects are too small to matter, and the hypothesis should therefore be set aside altogether.
B) complete disagreement: the effects are large, and have been established beyond reasonable doubt by many replications.
C) indifference: whether the effects exist is of little interest to a student of language, who has more important matters.
D) partial agreement: the effects are small, but their existence shows that language is more than a transparent medium.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Right about the size... wrong about their significance' is partial agreement. B and C go to the extremes; D contradicts the claim that the question is now an empirical one worth pursuing.

questions.passage:
Interviewer: Why does a car lose so much value the moment it leaves the showroom, even if it has barely been driven?

Economist: Part of it is ordinary depreciation, but most of the drop is information. The seller knows whether the car is a good one; the buyer does not. A buyer who knows that some of the cars on offer are problem cars, which their owners are keen to dump, will pay a price that reflects average quality, not the best. Owners of good cars, offered that average price, decline to sell, so the cars that remain are worse than average, and the price falls further. In the extreme the market unravels. That is Akerlof's lemons problem.

Interviewer: But used-car markets exist, and they function.

Economist: They do, because institutions have grown up to repair the information gap: warranties, certified pre-owned schemes, inspection reports, even the reputation of dealers who want repeat business. Notice that each of these works by making it costly for a seller of a bad car to imitate a seller of a good one. A warranty is worthless to someone who knows his car will break down, so offering one is a credible signal.
questions.question: According to the economist, the fall in a new car's value after it leaves the showroom is mainly explained by
options: A) buyers' inability to tell good cars from bad, which lowers the price they will pay for any used car.
B) ordinary depreciation, which is greatest during the first weeks of a car's life, whatever its condition may be.
C) owners of good cars who deliberately withdraw them from the market in order to push up the prices of used cars.
D) dealers who offer warranties on bad cars and so persuade buyers to pay more than the cars are really worth.
questions.explanation: Explanation: He says 'most of the drop is information': buyers cannot distinguish good from bad, so they pay for average quality. B contradicts 'most of the drop'; C reverses the cause (good owners withdraw because the price is low); D reverses the role of warranties.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Recent studies found that seawater reacts with the ash over centuries to grow crystals that seal cracks and strengthen the material.
2. Harbours built with it two thousand years ago still stand, while modern concrete in similar settings often decays within decades.
3. Roman engineers mixed volcanic ash with lime and seawater to make a concrete that hardened underwater.
4. The Romans, in other words, had made a concrete that improved with exposure to the very conditions that destroy ours.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 3 introduces the Roman mixture. 2 ('it') gives the evidence of durability. 1 ('Recent studies') explains why, and 4 ('in other words') restates the lesson. Order: 3-2-1-4.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. This is the winner's curse: victory itself is evidence that one's estimate was too high.
2. Rational bidders therefore shade their bids below their own estimates, and the more bidders there are, the more they must shade.
3. In an auction where bidders are unsure of an item's true value, the winner is usually the one who has most overestimated it.
4. Those who ignore the effect tend to win often and profit rarely.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 3 gives the setting. 1 ('This is the winner's curse') names the effect. 2 ('therefore') gives the rational response, and 4 describes those who ignore it. Order: 3-1-2-4.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Many other moons in the solar system have been locked in the same way to their planets.
2. The Earth itself is not exempt: the Moon is slowly slowing its rotation, lengthening the day by a fraction of a millisecond each century.
3. This is not a coincidence but the result of tidal forces, which slowed the Moon's rotation until it matched the time it takes to orbit the Earth.
4. The Moon always shows the same face to the Earth.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 4 states the fact. 3 ('This is not a coincidence') explains it. 1 ('in the same way') generalises to other moons, and 2 ('itself is not exempt') turns to the Earth. Order: 4-3-1-2.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. By that stage, most of the money has already been spent or withdrawn, and late investors recover little.
2. So long as new money keeps arriving, the returns look real and word of them spreads.
3. The scheme collapses when recruitment slows, because the promised payments then exceed the incoming funds.
4. A Ponzi scheme pays early investors with money from later ones rather than from genuine profits.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 4 defines the scheme. 2 ('So long as') describes its working phase. 3 describes the collapse, and 1 ('By that stage') describes its aftermath. Order: 4-2-3-1.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'The Condorcet jury theorem shows that if each member of a jury is more likely than not to judge correctly, the probability that the majority is right rises towards certainty as the jury grows. The theorem's force depends on an assumption that is easily violated: that the members' judgements are independent. If jurors are swayed by a common source of error, such as a persuasive but misleading expert, additional members add little; and if each is more likely wrong than right, the theorem works in reverse, making large majorities reliably mistaken.'
options: A) Large juries are always more accurate than small ones, since majorities become more certain as the number of jurors increases beyond a dozen.
B) The Condorcet theorem is false, because jurors are usually influenced by experts and so cannot be said to judge independently of one another.
C) Group majorities grow more reliable with size only if members beat chance and judge independently; otherwise they can be reliably wrong.
D) Jurors who are individually more likely to be wrong than right should be excluded from juries, since they make every majority unreliable.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph states the theorem and its two conditions (better than chance; independence) and the reversal when either fails. B drops the conditions; C says the theorem is false rather than conditional; D invents a recommendation.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Comparative advantage explains why trade can benefit a country that is worse than its partners at producing everything. What matters is not absolute productivity but opportunity cost: a country should specialise in what it gives up least to produce. The argument assumes, however, that resources can be moved without cost from declining industries to expanding ones. When workers cannot easily retrain or relocate, the gains are real but their distribution is lopsided, and those who lose may lose permanently.'
options: A) Trade gains rest on comparative advantage, but because adjustment is costly they may bring lasting losses to particular groups.
B) Countries that are worse at producing everything should not trade at all, since they cannot gain from specialising in any single industry.
C) Comparative advantage depends on absolute productivity, and so the more productive countries gain from trade at the expense of weaker ones.
D) Workers who lose their jobs to trade always find work in expanding industries, so that no group suffers any lasting harm as a result.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph gives the principle and then the hidden assumption of costless adjustment, with uneven and possibly permanent losses. B and C contradict the first sentences; D contradicts the last.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Memorials and monuments are usually understood as acts of remembrance, but they are equally acts of forgetting. To erect a statue to one figure is to select, from a crowded past, what a community will stop to look at; the choice implies a ranking, and the ranking silences. A monument that seems to speak for the whole community often speaks for those who commissioned it. This is why disputes over statues are rarely about the person depicted: they are about who is entitled to decide what is remembered.'
options: A) Statues should be removed from public spaces, because they inevitably misrepresent the persons whom they were erected to depict.
B) Monuments select as well as remember, so disputes over them concern who has the authority to decide what a community remembers.
C) Communities erect monuments in order to forget the past, and the people depicted in them are therefore of no importance to anyone.
D) Disputes over statues are about the personal character of the figures depicted, and not about the choices made by the community.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph argues that monuments select and silence, and that disputes are about who decides. B and C overstate; D says the opposite of the last sentence.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'Scientists often speak of a theory's predictive power, yet prediction alone is a poor test of understanding. ________ Ptolemaic astronomy predicted the positions of the planets with considerable accuracy for over a thousand years, and its epicycles could be adjusted to fit almost any observation. What it could not do was explain why the planets moved as they did, and it was this deficiency, rather than any failure of prediction, that eventually told against it.'
options: A) Accurate predictions are therefore worthless, and scientists should abandon the practice of testing theories against evidence.
B) Ptolemy's model was abandoned because it failed to predict the positions of the planets after the Middle Ages.
C) Theories that explain a phenomenon are always less accurate than theories that merely predict it, whatever the field.
D) A model can reproduce the data without capturing the mechanism that generates it.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The example shows prediction without explanation. B overgeneralises; C contradicts 'rather than any failure of prediction'; D overstates ('always').

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'Newspapers have long relied on advertising, not subscriptions, for most of their revenue. ________ A paper's readers are, in effect, its product, sold to advertisers; its customers are the firms that pay. When advertising moved online to platforms that could target individuals more precisely, the economic foundation of local journalism weakened even though the number of readers had not fallen.'
options: A) Readers therefore have no influence over what a newspaper publishes, since they pay nothing at all for the paper.
B) Subscriptions have always been more profitable than advertising, and papers that rely on advertising are poorly run.
C) The arrangement means that the people who read a paper are not the people who pay for it.
D) Online platforms are better at journalism than newspapers because they can target readers more precisely than papers.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The next sentence says readers are the product and advertisers the customers. B overstates; C and D introduce claims that the paragraph does not make.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'Every language has words for the people to whom one is related, and anthropologists once assumed that these reflect biological facts. ________ In many societies a mother's sister is called mother, and her children brother and sister, while a father's sister's children are classed as potential marriage partners. The terms follow rules of social obligation, not degrees of genetic closeness.'
options: A) Societies that call a mother's sister mother are ignorant of the biological facts of parenthood and descent.
B) Kinship terms, however, divide relatives according to social categories that need not match biology.
C) Genetic closeness has been shown to be the sole basis of the terms used for relatives in every society.
D) Anthropologists have since discovered that no society has words for relatives of any kind or description.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'However' signals a correction to the assumption, to be illustrated by the examples that follow. B, C and D contradict or distort the paragraph.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence:

The senator's ________ refusal to compromise, long after the votes had turned against him, was admired by his supporters as principle and condemned by his opponents as vanity.
options: A) quixotic
B) pragmatic
C) tentative
D) capricious
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Quixotic' means idealistic to the point of impracticality. 'Pragmatic' and 'tentative' contradict a refusal to compromise; 'capricious' (unpredictable) does not fit a consistent refusal.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence:

Her critics found her prose ________: it dazzled with ornament but, on inspection, said very little.
options: A) laconic
B) austere
C) lucid
D) florid
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Florid' means elaborately ornate. 'Laconic' and 'austere' describe plain, spare prose; 'lucid' means clear.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence:

The explanation was dismissed as post hoc, since ________.
options: A) it had been proposed by an eminent scholar several years before the event whose causes it was said to explain
B) it had been tested in a series of independent trials, each of which yielded a result consistent with its claims
C) it had been put together after the event to fit what had already happened, and predicted nothing new
D) it relied on evidence collected by the author's own research team over a period of more than twenty years
questions.explanation: Explanation: A post hoc explanation is built after the fact to fit known outcomes. Only the first option says that. The others describe prior proposal, independent testing and long collection of evidence.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best fills the blanks:

The theory's ________ appeal masked its ________ foundations, and critics who looked beyond the ________ found little to support it.
options: A) profound; flimsy; veneer
B) superficial; robust; veneer
C) superficial; flimsy; substance
D) superficial; flimsy; veneer
questions.explanation: Explanation: An appeal that 'masked' weak foundations is superficial; the foundations are flimsy, and the critics looked beyond the veneer (thin surface). 'Profound' and 'robust' do not fit 'masked'; 'looked beyond the substance' is illogical.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best fills the blanks:

He was famous for his ________ wit, which could ________ an opponent in a single sentence, yet in private he was ________ and kind.
options: A) caustic; devastate; gentle
B) genial; devastate; gentle
C) caustic; flatter; gentle
D) caustic; devastate; vindictive
questions.explanation: Explanation: Biting ('caustic') wit that could 'devastate' an opponent contrasts with a gentle private manner ('yet'). 'Genial' wit would not devastate; 'flatter' does not fit 'caustic'; 'vindictive' contradicts 'kind'.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: A) The treasurer's conduct was creditable, and the board commended her for it at the meeting.
B) Despite years of losses, the board remained sanguinary about the firm's prospects.
C) The faction's leader, a fractious man, split the party within a year of taking charge.
D) The account of the siege was graphic and sanguinary, and few readers could finish it.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Sanguine' means optimistic; 'sanguinary' means bloody, as correctly used in D. 'Creditable' (deserving praise) and 'fractious' (quarrelsome) are used correctly.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: A) The jury was asked to appraise the damage and to award appropriate compensation.
B) She was oblivious to the stares of the crowd as she walked slowly on.
C) The lawyer will apprise the value of the estate before it is offered for sale.
D) The two events were separated by a decade, and the link between them is tenuous.
questions.explanation: Explanation: To 'appraise' is to assess value; to 'apprise' is to inform. 'Appraise' in B, 'oblivious' (unaware) and 'tenuous' (slight) are used correctly.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'PUSILLANIMOUS':
options: A) Craven
B) Intrepid
C) Candid
D) Pompous
questions.explanation: Explanation: Pusillanimous means timid and lacking courage; 'craven' is closest. 'Intrepid' is the opposite.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'PERFIDIOUS':
options: A) Treacherous
B) Loyal
C) Devious
D) Insidious
questions.explanation: Explanation: Perfidious means deceitful and disloyal; 'loyal' is the antonym. The others are near-synonyms.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'RECONDITE':
options: A) Obvious
B) Frivolous
C) Notorious
D) Abstruse
questions.explanation: Explanation: Recondite means little known and hard to understand; 'abstruse' is closest. 'Obvious' is the opposite.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'SALUBRIOUS':
options: A) Health-giving
B) Wholesome
C) Noxious
D) Invigorating
questions.explanation: Explanation: Salubrious means health-giving; 'noxious' (harmful) is the antonym. The others are near-synonyms.

questions.question:
Choose the correct meaning of the idiom:
'To rest on one's laurels' means to:
options: A) receive public honours in recognition of a lifetime of faithful service to an institution
B) be content with past achievements instead of seeking new ones
C) take a long holiday after the completion of a project that has been difficult and tiring
D) claim credit for the achievements of colleagues in order to advance one's own career in the firm
questions.explanation: Explanation: To rest on one's laurels is to rely on past success and make no further effort.

questions.question: Select the sentence in which 'CENSURE' is used correctly:
options: A) The board voted to censure the director for concealing the losses.
B) The film was subject to censure, and three scenes were cut before it was released to the public.
C) The ministry will censure the magazine's contents before they are permitted to be published in the capital.
D) She was careful to censure her emails for any hint of the dispute before sending them on to the committee.
questions.explanation: Explanation: To 'censure' is to criticise formally. The sense of cutting or suppressing material in B, C and D belongs to 'censor'.

questions.question:
Choose the best replacement for the underlined portion:

Not until the results were published <u>the researchers realised</u> that the sample had been biased.
options: A) had the researchers realised
B) the researchers had realised
C) were the researchers realising
D) did the researchers realise
questions.explanation: Explanation: A fronted negative expression ('Not until...') requires subject-auxiliary inversion in the main clause: 'did the researchers realise'.

questions.question:
Choose the best replacement for the underlined portion:

Had she known about the delay, she <u>would leave</u> earlier.
options: A) would be leaving
B) will have left
C) would have left
D) had left
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Had she known' is a third conditional, which requires 'would have' plus the past participle in the main clause.

questions.question:
Spot the error in the following sentence:
'The principal reason (A) / for the delay was (B) / because the funds (C) / had not been released (D).'
options: A) The principal reason
B) for the delay was
C) because the funds
D) had not been released
questions.explanation: Explanation: After 'the reason... was', the clause should be introduced by 'that', not 'because': 'was that the funds had not been released'.

questions.question:
Spot the error in the following sentence:
'Each of the participants (A) / were asked (B) / to sign a consent form (C) / before the trial began (D).'
options: A) Each of the participants
B) were asked
C) to sign a consent form
D) before the trial began
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Each' is singular, so the verb should be 'was asked'.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
options: A) Seldom I have seen such determination in so young a player of the game.
B) Seldom did I saw such determination in so young a player of the game.
C) Seldom have I seen so determination in so young player of the game.
D) Seldom have I seen such determination in so young a player.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A fronted negative adverb ('seldom') requires inversion of auxiliary and subject: 'Seldom have I seen'.

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'She would rather he ________ her the truth than hide it.'
options: A) told
B) tell
C) tells
D) had tell
questions.explanation: Explanation: After 'would rather' with a different subject, the past subjunctive form is used: 'would rather he told'.

questions.question: Identify the grammatically INCORRECT sentence:
options: A) Neither of the answers given by the candidate is correct.
B) A number of students has applied for the scholarship.
C) The number of applicants has risen sharply over the last year.
D) Everyone in the room was surprised by the announcement.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'A number of' takes a plural verb: 'have applied'. The other sentences agree correctly ('the number of' is singular).

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'The success of the plan is contingent ________ the approval of the board.'
options: A) on
B) with
C) to
D) by
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Contingent' takes 'on' (or 'upon').

questions.passage:
In the autumn of 1973 the University of California, Berkeley, admitted 44 per cent of its male applicants to graduate school and only 35 per cent of its female applicants. The gap was large enough to look like discrimination, and when statisticians examined the figures department by department they found something stranger: in most of the large departments, women were admitted at rates equal to or slightly higher than those of men. The explanation, once seen, was simple. Women had applied in larger numbers to departments that rejected most applicants, while men had applied in larger numbers to departments that admitted many. The aggregate figure mixed two things, the behaviour of the admitting departments and the choices of the applicants, and the mixture pointed in a direction that neither component did.

This reversal is called Simpson's paradox, and it is not confined to universities. In a study of treatments for kidney stones, one method succeeded more often than the other for small stones and also for large stones, yet appeared worse when the two groups of patients were pooled. The reason was that doctors tended to give the more invasive treatment to patients with large stones, which are harder to treat by any method, so that the apparently inferior method had been tried on harder cases. Arithmetic does not forbid such reversals; it requires them whenever the groups being compared differ in the mix of cases they contain.

The textbook moral is to disaggregate: look inside the groups before drawing conclusions from the whole. But the moral is incomplete, for it suggests that the subgroup figures are always the truer ones, and that is not so. Suppose a drug lowers blood pressure, and blood pressure in turn affects the risk of a heart attack. Comparing patients within groups of equal blood pressure would then hide the drug's benefit, since the drug works through blood pressure; the pooled figures, not the subgroup figures, would answer the question a patient wants answered. Which table to trust depends on what caused what, and the numbers do not say.

The Berkeley case illustrates the difficulty. Suppose that the departments were neutral, and that women chose harder departments because they had been discouraged, at earlier stages, from the subjects that admit more readily. Then the department-level figures show no bias at the point of admission, yet the system as a whole disadvantages women, through a cause that operates before the application is submitted. Suppose instead that women simply preferred those subjects and the system was fair. The admissions figures are the same in both stories. What differs is the causal account of why the applicants distributed themselves as they did, and no table can reveal it. A statistician who says the paradox has been resolved by looking within departments has therefore answered one question, whether the departments discriminated, and left a second, whether the university's applicants faced unequal obstacles, untouched.

This is why the paradox has attracted philosophers as much as statisticians. It exposes the fact that statistical association, however precisely measured, does not by itself determine causal conclusions, and that the choice of which variables to hold constant is a causal decision disguised as a technical one. Practitioners sometimes respond by adopting a rule, such as always adjusting for every available variable, but such rules fail: adjusting for the wrong variable can create a bias where none existed. Others insist that causal claims should rest on randomised experiments, in which the assignment of treatment is independent of the characteristics of the cases. Randomisation does remove the problem, but it is often impossible, as when the treatment is gender, or a policy introduced everywhere at once.

None of this makes data useless. It makes them dependent on assumptions that the analyst must state and defend, which is a discipline and not a defeat. A figure presented without its causal story invites readers to supply one of their own, and they usually supply the story that flatters their prior opinion. The remedy is to ask, of any comparison, what else differs between the groups, and whether that difference lies on the path through which the supposed cause is thought to operate.
questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?
options: A) Simpson's paradox shows that aggregate data are always misleading, and that analysts should therefore rely only on figures within subgroups of the data.
B) Statistical comparisons cannot be interpreted without causal assumptions, since whether to aggregate or disaggregate depends on what caused what.
C) The Berkeley data demonstrate that the university's departments discriminated against women, though in ways that were hidden by the averaging of rates.
D) Randomised experiments are the only legitimate source of causal knowledge, and observational data should therefore be disregarded by careful analysts.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage argues that disaggregating is not always right; which table to trust 'depends on what caused what'. B contradicts the blood-pressure example; C reverses the Berkeley finding (departments showed no bias); D overstates the case for experiments, which the author calls often impossible.

Around 1200 BCE the eastern Mediterranean, which had been a web of palace states trading in tin, copper, grain, textiles and luxury goods, came apart within a few decades. The Hittite capital was abandoned. The port of Ugarit on the Syrian coast was destroyed and never rebuilt. The Mycenaean palaces of Greece were burned, and with them vanished the system of records on which their administration depended; literacy itself disappeared from Greece for centuries. Egypt survived, though shaken, and records the defeat of invaders, whom it called the Sea Peoples, by Ramesses III in about 1177 BCE. Within a generation, a world of great powers in constant diplomatic correspondence had been replaced by smaller, poorer and more isolated societies.

The search for a cause began early, and for a long time it produced single answers. The Egyptian inscriptions pointed to invaders from the sea, and for generations the Sea Peoples were blamed. Later scholars proposed an earthquake storm, a sequence of seismic shocks along the great fault lines of the region; prolonged drought, inferred from pollen and sediment records; famine; and internal revolt against the palace elites. Each had some evidence, and none sufficed. Earthquakes can destroy a city but do not explain why it was not rebuilt; drought explains hunger but not why states in wetter regions fell; and the Sea Peoples, who appear in Egyptian reliefs as migrants with families and ox-carts, look less like the cause of the collapse than a symptom of the displacement that accompanied it.

The now favoured explanation is multi-causal. On this account the late Bronze Age states were bound together by trade, tribute and marriage alliances, so tightly that each depended on the others for things it could not produce, tin above all, since bronze requires it and it came from few and distant sources. Interdependence made the system efficient while it held, but fragile when it did not: a shock that an isolated state would have absorbed spread through the network, and several shocks arriving together overwhelmed its capacity to adapt. A drought could cut harvests, famine could unsettle populations and set them moving, migrants could threaten trade routes, and the loss of trade could deprive palaces of the goods that sustained their authority. The collapse was, in this telling, a cascade.

This is persuasive, but it has a weakness that deserves attention. An explanation that allows any combination of drought, earthquakes, invasion and revolt to contribute is hard to test, since no evidence can count against it. The explanation risks becoming a way of describing what happened and not of accounting for why. The more serious test is comparative. Egypt and Assyria, both deeply involved in the same networks, survived, while others did not. A good explanation must say why, and the candidate answers, such as Egypt's concentrated agricultural wealth in the Nile valley, its centralised army and its geographical protection, are plausible but need to be shown and not assumed.

Another objection concerns the word collapse. The destruction was real, but historians increasingly stress that it was uneven, and that its apparent suddenness owes much to the nature of the evidence. A palace that kept archives leaves a dramatic record of its fall; a village that quietly adapted leaves almost nothing. Where life continued, as in parts of Cyprus and the Levantine coast, it did so in altered forms, and some of the societies that emerged, among them the Phoenician cities, benefited from the disruption, since the removal of the great powers gave them room to grow.

The episode has attracted attention beyond ancient history because it appears to warn us about modern complexity. The analogy should be handled carefully. What it suggests is not that complex systems inevitably fail, but that the features that make them productive can also carry the damage of one failure to the rest, and that resilience may lie in redundancy, in having more than one source for what is essential. Whether societies that can see such risks are willing to pay the cost of insuring against them is a question the Bronze Age leaves open, as it remains open for us.

The Mycenaean palaces of Greece were burned, and with them vanished the system of records on which their administration depended; literacy itself disappeared from Greece for centuries. Egypt survived, though shaken, and records the defeat of invaders, whom it called the Sea Peoples, by Ramesses III in about 1177 BCE. Within a generation, a world of great powers in constant diplomatic correspondence had been replaced by smaller, poorer and more isolated societies.

The search for a cause began early, and for a long time it produced single answers. The Egyptian inscriptions pointed to invaders from the sea, and for generations the Sea Peoples were blamed. Later scholars proposed an earthquake storm, a sequence of seismic shocks along the great fault lines of the region; prolonged drought, inferred from pollen and sediment records; famine; and internal revolt against the palace elites. Each had some evidence, and none sufficed. Earthquakes can destroy a city but do not explain why it was not rebuilt; drought explains hunger but not why states in wetter regions fell; and the Sea Peoples, who appear in Egyptian reliefs as migrants with families and ox-carts, look less like the cause of the collapse than a symptom of the displacement that accompanied it.

The now favoured explanation is multi-causal. On this account the late Bronze Age states were bound together by trade, tribute and marriage alliances, so tightly that each depended on the others for things it could not produce, tin above all, since bronze requires it and it came from few and distant sources. Interdependence made the system efficient while it held, but fragile when it did not: a shock that an isolated state would have absorbed spread through the network, and several shocks arriving together overwhelmed its capacity to adapt. A drought could cut harvests, famine could unsettle populations and set them moving, migrants could threaten trade routes, and the loss of trade could deprive palaces of the goods that sustained their authority. The collapse was, in this telling, a cascade.

This is persuasive, but it has a weakness that deserves attention. An explanation that allows any combination of drought, earthquakes, invasion and revolt to contribute is hard to test, since no evidence can count against it. The explanation risks becoming a way of describing what happened and not of accounting for why. The more serious test is comparative. Egypt and Assyria, both deeply involved in the same networks, survived, while others did not. A good explanation must say why, and the candidate answers, such as Egypt's concentrated agricultural wealth in the Nile valley, its centralised army and its geographical protection, are plausible but need to be shown and not assumed.

Another objection concerns the word collapse. The destruction was real, but historians increasingly stress that it was uneven, and that its apparent suddenness owes much to the nature of the evidence. A palace that kept archives leaves a dramatic record of its fall; a village that quietly adapted leaves almost nothing. Where life continued, as in parts of Cyprus and the Levantine coast, it did so in altered forms, and some of the societies that emerged, among them the Phoenician cities, benefited from the disruption, since the removal of the great powers gave them room to grow.

The episode has attracted attention beyond ancient history because it appears to warn us about modern complexity. The analogy should be handled carefully. What it suggests is not that complex systems inevitably fail, but that the features that make them productive can also carry the damage of one failure to the rest, and that resilience may lie in redundancy, in having more than one source for what is essential. Whether societies that can see such risks are willing to pay the cost of insuring against them is a question the Bronze Age leaves open, as it remains open for us.

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the analogy with modern complexity is best described as
options: A) dismissive: the Bronze Age has nothing to teach us about the risks of interdependence in the modern world.
B) alarmed: modern societies are bound to collapse in the way that the Bronze Age states did.

questions.passage:
Interviewer: People worry that our era will leave less trace than the Middle Ages, because digital files vanish. Is that fair?

Archivist: Half fair. A parchment can sit in a cellar for five hundred years and still be read. A file can be unreadable in twenty, not because the bits decay, though they can, but because nobody can run the software that interprets them. The threat is obsolescence more than decay. But the opposite problem is as real: we are producing more records than any period in history and cannot keep or index all of them, so future historians may drown rather than starve.

Interviewer: So what should be saved?

Archivist: That is the uncomfortable question, because preservation is selection, and selection is judgement made on behalf of people who do not yet exist. The least bad policy is to keep original formats along with the documentation needed to interpret them, and to be generous about what counts as worth keeping, since the things later generations value are often the dull ones: price lists, parish registers, shipping manifests.
questions.question: According to the archivist, the main threat to digital records is
options: A) the obsolescence of the software needed to interpret files, more than their physical decay.
B) the physical decay of storage media, which makes files unreadable within a few years of their creation.
C) the deliberate deletion of records by institutions that wish to conceal their activities from historians.
D) the shortage of historians who are trained to interpret the records produced by modern institutions.
questions.explanation: Explanation: He says 'the threat is obsolescence more than decay'. B contradicts this; C and D are not mentioned.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'A recurring puzzle in medicine is that treatments tested in trials often fail to deliver in routine practice. Trial participants are selected for being likely to benefit and to adhere, are monitored closely, and are free of other conditions; ordinary patients are none of these. A drug's efficacy, the effect under ideal conditions, thus differs from its effectiveness, the effect in the world, and the gap between them is not a flaw in the trial but a consequence of what it was designed to isolate.'
options: A) Clinical trials are unreliable because their participants are closely monitored, and doctors should therefore ignore the results of every trial.
B) A drug that works in a trial will work equally well in routine practice, since the trial has already established its effect beyond doubt.
C) Trials measure efficacy under ideal conditions, so results can overstate what a treatment does for ordinary patients.
D) Ordinary patients gain more from drugs than trial participants do, because trials exclude those who are the most severely ill.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph distinguishes efficacy from effectiveness and says the gap follows from the trial's design. B and C contradict this; D reverses the direction of the gap.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Economic historians once explained the early industrialisation of Britain by its coal and its colonies. Recent work places more weight on a less visible resource: high wages. Because labour was expensive relative to energy, British manufacturers had an unusual incentive to invent machines that saved labour and used coal, whereas elsewhere, where labour was cheap, the same machines would not have repaid their cost. On this view, the Industrial Revolution was less a matter of what Britain had than of what its prices made worth inventing.'
options: A) Britain's industrialisation is increasingly explained by high wages relative to energy, which made labour-saving inventions profitable.
B) Britain industrialised first because it had cheap labour, which allowed its manufacturers to produce goods at lower cost than their rivals could.
C) Coal and colonies had nothing to do with British industrialisation, as economic historians have now shown to be beyond any doubt.
D) The Industrial Revolution happened in Britain because its inventors were more talented than those of other countries in the same period.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph shifts weight from coal and colonies to relative prices, with high wages encouraging labour-saving machines. B reverses 'expensive labour'; C overstates ('nothing to do'); D invents a claim.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'The ancient Greeks distinguished between two words for time. Chronos was the time of the clock and the calendar, uniform and measurable; kairos was the right or opportune moment, qualitative and unrepeatable. Modern life privileges the first, and our tools, from schedules to stopwatches, are built for it. But much that matters, such as when to speak, when to act and when to wait, is a matter of kairos, and no calendar can tell us when it has come.'
options: A) The ancient Greeks had no clocks and so could not measure time accurately, a defect that modern tools have since remedied in full.
B) Greek separated measurable time from the opportune moment, and modern tools favour the former though much depends on the latter.
C) Kairos and chronos were equally prized by the Greeks, and modern life gives equal weight to both kinds of time in practice.
D) Calendars and schedules should be abandoned, since they prevent people from recognising the right moment in which to act.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph contrasts chronos and kairos and notes that modern tools suit chronos while important decisions turn on kairos. The others distort or overstate this.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'It is natural to suppose that a more severe punishment deters more crime. ________ Offenders, studies suggest, are far more sensitive to the likelihood of being caught than to the length of the sentence, partly because those who commit crimes tend to discount the future heavily and partly because they expect not to be caught. Doubling the sentence for a crime that is rarely detected changes little; raising the chance of detection changes a great deal.'
options: A) Severe punishments should therefore be abolished, since they have never been shown to reduce any form of crime.
B) Offenders who are caught are always sentenced to the maximum term, and so severity cannot be said to differ.
C) Detection rates are determined by the severity of sentences, and so the two are in effect one and the same factor.
D) The evidence, however, suggests that the certainty of punishment matters more than its severity.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The next sentences say offenders respond to the likelihood of being caught more than to severity. B, C and D contradict or distort this.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'A map is useful because it leaves things out. ________ A map that recorded every tree and every paving stone would be as big as the country and as hard to read, and would defeat its purpose of letting us find our way. The art of the cartographer lies in deciding what to omit, and every such decision reflects a view of what the map is for.'
options: A) Maps are therefore inaccurate, and should not be trusted by travellers who wish to find their way in unfamiliar country.
B) Cartographers omit features at random, since no principle exists for deciding which details deserve to be shown on a map.
C) Its value lies in simplification, and a map fully faithful to the terrain would be worthless.
D) The best map is always the largest one, since it contains the greatest number of details about the country that it shows.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The following sentences show that completeness would defeat a map's purpose. B, C and D contradict or distort the paragraph.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'Why do some pieces of music give us chills? ________ Studies of listeners who report such responses find that the effect is strongest at moments when an expectation is set up and then violated, as when a melody swerves from the note we predicted, and brain scans show activity in regions linked with reward. The pleasure appears to arise less from the notes themselves than from the interplay between prediction and surprise.'
options: A) The reason is unknown, and no scientific study has ever produced any evidence that bears on the question.
B) One influential account locates the answer in the way music plays with our expectations.
C) Chills are caused by the volume of the music, and so quiet pieces cannot produce any such response at all.
D) Only trained musicians ever experience such responses, since they alone can predict how a melody will continue.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The sentences that follow report the role of expectation and surprise. B contradicts 'studies'; C and D are not supported.

The minister's reply was a model of ________: lengthy, courteous and entirely without content.
options: A) prevarication
B) brevity
C) candour
D) forthrightness
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Prevarication' is speaking evasively. 'Brevity', 'candour' and 'forthrightness' contradict 'lengthy' and 'without content'.

The old regime's apparent stability proved ________: it rested on fear, and vanished when the fear did.
options: A) durable
B) resilient
C) venerable
D) illusory
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Illusory' means deceptive and unreal. The other options suggest real strength or long standing.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence:

The merger was described as a marriage of convenience, since ________.
options: A) the two firms had worked closely together for several decades and held the same long-term strategy
B) the founders of both firms were related by marriage and had planned the merger since their childhood
C) neither firm shared the other's aims, and each stood to gain only in the short term
D) the shareholders of both firms had voted unanimously for the merger after a long period of consultation
questions.explanation: Explanation: A marriage of convenience is an arrangement made for advantage without real affinity. Only the first option fits. The others describe shared aims, family ties or consensus.

B) austere; invited; adornment
C) austere; resisted; moderation

options: A) ruthless; betray; courted
B) unassuming; betray; courted
C) ruthless; champion; courted
D) ruthless; betray; disdained

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: A) The committee's report was a model of clarity, and its conclusions were widely praised by the press.
B) The firm continued to flaunt safety rules despite repeated warnings.
C) She had a principled objection to the scheme, which she explained to the board at some length.
D) The siren sounded continuously for an hour before it was finally switched off by the guard on duty.
questions.explanation: Explanation: To disregard a rule openly is to 'flout' it; 'flaunt' means to show off. 'Clarity', 'principled' and 'continuously' are used correctly.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: A) The government's precipitous decision to devalue the currency alarmed investors and foreign creditors alike.
B) The professor was famous for his lucid explanations of difficult ideas to students of every level.
C) The climber made a precipitous descent down the sheer face of the mountain in the failing light.
D) He dissembled when asked about the money, pretending that he knew nothing of the transfer at all.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'OBSEQUIOUS':
options: A) Servile
B) Defiant
C) Taciturn
D) Capricious

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'ASCETIC':

B) Sybaritic
C) Austere

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'PERSPICACIOUS':
options: A) Garrulous
B) Gullible
C) Vindictive
D) Astute

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'EQUANIMITY':
options: A) Composure
B) Serenity
C) Agitation
D) Imperturbability

questions.question:

'To play devil's advocate' means to:

In 1937 the Boijmans Museum in Rotterdam bought a painting called Christ at Emmaus for a sum equivalent to millions today, on the strength of the judgement of the eminent Vermeer scholar Abraham Bredius, who called it a masterpiece. It was a forgery by Han van Meegeren, a painter with a grievance against the critics who had dismissed his own work. Van Meegeren's later career was extraordinary. He sold another false Vermeer to Hermann Goering, and when after the war he was charged with having sold the national heritage to the enemy, he escaped a charge of treason only by confessing to forgery and painting a further Vermeer in the presence of witnesses to prove it.

The episode poses a puzzle about value. The paintings had not changed. If viewers admired the Emmaus as a work of beauty, and its beauty lay in what could be seen on the canvas, then the discovery that it had been painted in 1936 and not 1660 should have left that admiration undisturbed. Yet it did not. Critics who had praised its spiritual depth now found its figures awkward and its sentiment cheap, and some noted, with hindsight, that its faces resembled the film actresses of the day. Either the earlier critics had been foolish, or knowledge of origin alters what we see.

Two broad answers have been given. The first holds that the aesthetic value of a work lies wholly in its perceptible qualities, and that the apparent change in the forgery's value reflects only the collapse of an illusion: critics, believing in a Vermeer, saw what a Vermeer should have, and when the belief went, so did the illusion. On this view a perfect forgery, one that no one could ever detect, would be as good as the original. The second answer denies that a work's value lies in its appearance alone. A painting, it says, is an achievement, the product of an act performed by a particular person at a particular time and we appreciate what is done as well as what is seen. Vermeer's handling of light was a discovery in the seventeenth century; a painter who copies it in the twentieth has discovered nothing.

The philosopher Nelson Goodman gave the dispute a precise form. Some arts, such as painting, are autographic: the distinction between original and copy matters, because the work is the particular object. Others, such as music and literature, are allographic: a score or a text can be reproduced in any number of copies without loss of authenticity, since the work consists in a structure that the copies share. Nobody asks whether a printed copy of a novel is a forgery. The test, Goodman suggested, is whether the history of production is relevant to what counts as the work.

This is a distinction and not an explanation, and it invites an objection. If the decision that history of production matters is merely conventional, then forgeries are condemned by a convention that could as easily be reversed. A defender of authenticity must therefore say why the convention is reasonable. One answer, due to Kendall Walton, is that we perceive works as belonging to categories, and that the same visible features are different in different categories: a distortion of the face that is daring in an Expressionist portrait is incompetence in a Dutch interior. We cannot see what a painting is doing without knowing when and by whom it was painted. A forgery in the style of Vermeer is therefore a different object of perception from a Vermeer, even where the two look the same, because the same marks mean different things.

The upshot is that the forger's success does not show that the concern with authenticity is mere snobbery. It shows that our responses to art are shaped by beliefs about its origin, and the question is whether that shaping is a distortion or part of what appreciation consists in. In 1912 the German meteorologist Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents had once formed a single landmass, which he later called Pangaea, and had since drifted apart. The idea was not wholly new; mapmakers had long remarked on the jigsaw fit of the coasts of South America and Africa. Wegener's contribution was to assemble evidence from several fields. Fossils of the same freshwater reptile, Mesosaurus, and of the same fern, Glossopteris, were found on continents now separated by oceans; rock formations and mountain chains on one side of the Atlantic continued on the other; and glacial deposits some 300 million years old lay in regions now close to the equator. No explanation based on land bridges or sunken continents, Wegener argued, could account for all of this as economically as drift.

The reception was hostile. At a symposium in New York in 1926 most of the geologists present rejected the theory, and for decades afterwards it was treated as a curiosity. The episode is often told as a story of a conservative establishment crushing a visionary,. But the objections were not frivolous. The decisive one concerned mechanism. Wegener suggested that continents ploughed through the rock of the ocean floor, driven by the Earth's rotation and the pull of the sun and moon, and physicists calculated that such forces were far too weak to move continents through rock that was solid and strong. A theory that asserts a motion but cannot supply a force to produce it is, on any sensible view, incomplete.

Defenders of the establishment's response can say more. Theories are accepted on the strength of what they explain as well as rejected for what they cannot, and the rival fixist accounts, could explain much of the same evidence with the tools then available: land bridges for the fossils, and the contraction of a cooling Earth for the mountains. When the evidence is compatible with a rival account that conflicts with no known physics, it is reasonable to prefer that account until the evidence becomes decisive. The geologists who rejected drift were applying a standard that they would have applied to a theory of their own.

What changed was not the argument but the data. After the Second World War, the mapping of the ocean floor revealed a continuous mid-ocean ridge and deep trenches; and in the early 1960s Harry Hess proposed that new crust forms at the ridges and spreads outward, with old crust consumed at the trenches. The decisive confirmation came from magnetic stripes on the sea floor, symmetrical on either side of the ridge, which recorded the reversals of the Earth's magnetic field as the new crust cooled. These observations supplied both a mechanism, the movement of the sea floor and not of continents ploughing through it, and a test, a prediction that could have failed. By the end of the 1960s plate tectonics, which absorbed drift into a larger theory, was generally accepted.

There are two tempting lessons, and both are wrong. The first is that scientists are hostile to new ideas, so that dissent should be presumed to be insight. The Wegener story has been invoked by many cranks who hope that rejection is itself a sign of vindication; but for each Wegener there are a great many people whose ideas were rejected because they were mistaken, and rejection by itself carries no information about which kind of case one is in. The second lesson, that the geologists were simply right to wait for a mechanism, overlooks the fact that the demand for a mechanism has sometimes been used to resist true theories: Darwin's account of evolution, to take one case, was accepted long before heredity was understood.

What the case does show is how much depends on the standards of evidence being applied. Wegener was right about the facts and wrong about the force, and in the circumstances of the 1920s there was no way for contemporaries to separate the two. A fairer judgement is that the resistance was reasonable, that it was also slow, and that the slowness was the price of a caution that protects science from error more often than it delays its progress.

The idea was not wholly new; mapmakers had long remarked on the jigsaw fit of the coasts of South America and Africa. Wegener's contribution was to assemble evidence from several fields. Fossils of the same freshwater reptile, Mesosaurus, and of the same fern, Glossopteris, were found on continents now separated by oceans; rock formations and mountain chains on one side of the Atlantic continued on the other; and glacial deposits some 300 million years old lay in regions now close to the equator. No explanation based on land bridges or sunken continents, Wegener argued, could account for all of this as economically as drift.

The reception was hostile. At a symposium in New York in 1926 most of the geologists present rejected the theory, and for decades afterwards it was treated as a curiosity. The episode is often told as a story of a conservative establishment crushing a visionary,. But the objections were not frivolous. The decisive one concerned mechanism. Wegener suggested that continents ploughed through the rock of the ocean floor, driven by the Earth's rotation and the pull of the sun and moon, and physicists calculated that such forces were far too weak to move continents through rock that was solid and strong. A theory that asserts a motion but cannot supply a force to produce it is, on any sensible view, incomplete.

Defenders of the establishment's response can say more. Theories are accepted on the strength of what they explain as well as rejected for what they cannot, and the rival fixist accounts, could explain much of the same evidence with the tools then available: land bridges for the fossils, and the contraction of a cooling Earth for the mountains. When the evidence is compatible with a rival account that conflicts with no known physics, it is reasonable to prefer that account until the evidence becomes decisive. The geologists who rejected drift were applying a standard that they would have applied to a theory of their own.

What changed was not the argument but the data. After the Second World War, the mapping of the ocean floor revealed a continuous mid-ocean ridge and deep trenches; and in the early 1960s Harry Hess proposed that new crust forms at the ridges and spreads outward, with old crust consumed at the trenches. The decisive confirmation came from magnetic stripes on the sea floor, symmetrical on either side of the ridge, which recorded the reversals of the Earth's magnetic field as the new crust cooled. These observations supplied both a mechanism, the movement of the sea floor and not of continents ploughing through it, and a test, a prediction that could have failed. By the end of the 1960s plate tectonics, which absorbed drift into a larger theory, was generally accepted.

There are two tempting lessons, and both are wrong. The first is that scientists are hostile to new ideas, so that dissent should be presumed to be insight. The Wegener story has been invoked by many cranks who hope that rejection is itself a sign of vindication; but for each Wegener there are a great many people whose ideas were rejected because they were mistaken, and rejection by itself carries no information about which kind of case one is in. The second lesson, that the geologists were simply right to wait for a mechanism, overlooks the fact that the demand for a mechanism has sometimes been used to resist true theories: Darwin's account of evolution, to take one case, was accepted long before heredity was understood.

What the case does show is how much depends on the standards of evidence being applied. Wegener was right about the facts and wrong about the force, and in the circumstances of the 1920s there was no way for contemporaries to separate the two. A fairer judgement is that the resistance was reasonable, that it was also slow, and that the slowness was the price of a caution that protects science from error more often than it delays its progress.

Interviewer: Starting school later seems like a simple fix for tired teenagers. Is it?

Scientist: It is a good fix for a real problem, but it is not as simple as it sounds. Adolescents' body clocks shift later at puberty, so asking a sixteen-year-old to be alert at half past seven is like asking an adult to be alert at five. Trials of later start times show more sleep, fewer late arrivals and, in several studies, better attendance. What is less clear is the effect on grades. The results are mixed, and the best studies are small.

Interviewer: Why mixed?

Scientist: Partly because schools that move the start time often change other things at the same time, so you cannot isolate the effect, and partly because teenagers given an extra hour sometimes just go to bed an hour later, which cancels the gain. The policy works only if the evenings do not shift too. That is why I tell schools to pair it with advice on screens and bedtimes, and to measure sleep itself, not just grades.
questions.question: According to the scientist, the evidence on later school start times is
options: A) clear on sleep and attendance but mixed on grades.
B) clear on grades and attendance but uncertain on the amount of sleep that teenagers get.
C) conclusive on every measure, since the best studies of the question have been large ones.
D) too weak to support any conclusion, because no trial has measured the sleep of students.
questions.explanation: Explanation: He says trials show more sleep, fewer late arrivals and better attendance in several studies, while the effect on grades is mixed. The others misstate this.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Reciprocity is among the most reliable of human social norms: we feel obliged to return favours, and gifts create debts. The obligation is strong enough to be exploited. Charities that enclose a small gift with an appeal for donations raise more money than those that do not, and salespeople offer free samples. But the norm can also be corrupted by being made too explicit: a gift that is immediately matched with a payment ceases to be a gift and becomes a trade, and the warmth that sustained the relationship is lost.'
options: A) Charities should enclose gifts with their appeals, since this is the only reliable means of raising money from the members of the public.
B) Gifts and trades are the same thing, and the obligation to return favours is a fiction invented by salespeople and by charities.
C) Reciprocity binds through obligation and can be exploited, but made explicit it becomes a mere trade and loses its warmth.
D) People feel no obligation to return favours unless they have first been given something of real value by the person who asks.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph states the norm, its exploitation, and its corruption when made explicit. B, C and D overstate or invert these points.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Many plant species depend on animals to disperse their seeds, and the loss of those animals can doom the plants even when the plants themselves are not threatened directly. Large fruit-eating birds and mammals, which swallow big seeds and deposit them far from the parent, are especially vulnerable to hunting; when they vanish, large-seeded trees are left to drop their fruit beneath their own crowns, where seedlings compete with their parents and attract pests. The forest may look intact for decades, though its composition is slowly changing.'
options: A) Losing large seed dispersers can quietly alter forests that still look intact, as large-seeded trees cannot spread.
B) Large fruit-eating animals are hunted because they eat the seeds of valuable trees, and forests should be protected from them.
C) Trees that drop their fruit beneath their own crowns are the most successful species in the tropical forests of the world.
D) Forests that look intact are always in good health, and the loss of animals has no effect on the plants that live there.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph traces how losing dispersers changes forests slowly and invisibly. The other options invent or reverse claims.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Modern cities are often described as engines of innovation, and there is evidence that patents and productivity rise with city size. The explanation usually offered is that density speeds the exchange of ideas. But cities also select: they attract ambitious and talented people who would be productive anywhere, and their high costs deter others. Separating the effect of the place from the effect of the people is difficult, since people sort themselves among places for reasons that are related to their abilities.'
options: A) Cities make everyone who lives in them more productive, since the exchange of ideas is faster in places where people are dense.
B) Innovation rises with city size, but talented people sort into cities, so the city's own effect is hard to isolate.
C) Large cities are less innovative than small towns, since high costs deter talented people from choosing to live in them.
D) Patents and productivity are unrelated to the size of a city, and the apparent link is merely an artefact of how they are counted.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph gives the usual explanation and then the selection problem. B ignores the problem; C and D contradict the first sentence.
