In 1999 a solicitor named Sally Clark was convicted of murdering her two infant sons. The case against her rested heavily on testimony from a distinguished paediatrician, who told the jury that the chance of two cot deaths occurring in a family like hers was one in 73 million. He obtained the figure by taking the published frequency of a single cot death in such a family, about one in 8,543, and multiplying it by itself. Clark's conviction was upheld on a first appeal in 2000 and quashed only in 2003, after she had spent more than three years in prison.

The figure contained two separate mistakes. The first was an error about independence. Multiplying probabilities is legitimate only when events are independent, and there are reasons to think that cot deaths in one family are not: genetic or environmental factors that made one death more likely would make a second more likely too. The true chance of a second cot death in such a family was therefore probably far higher than the chance of a first in an arbitrary one. But this was not the more instructive error.

The second mistake was one of logic, and has a name: the prosecutor's fallacy. Even if the figure had been correct, it would have answered the wrong question. One in 73 million was supposed to be the probability that two babies would die naturally, which is the probability of the evidence if the mother were innocent. What the jury needed was the probability that the mother was innocent, given the evidence. The two are not the same, and confusing them is as natural as it is dangerous. The chance that someone who has been struck by lightning was outdoors is very high; the chance that someone outdoors will be struck is very low.

To answer the right question one must compare explanations. Two babies dying naturally in one family is extremely rare; so is a mother murdering two of her children. Both explanations are improbable, and the evidence is that one of them occurred. The sensible question is therefore which is the less improbable, and that requires estimating the frequency of double murder as well as that of double cot death. When statisticians attempted this, they concluded that, on the figures available, a double natural death was at least as probable as a double murder, and perhaps considerably more so. The very rarity that appeared to condemn Clark applied equally to the case against her.

There was a further circumstance. Evidence of a bacterial infection in the second child, which might have supported a natural explanation, had not been disclosed to the defence by the pathologist, and its discovery was a ground for the second appeal. The statistical error was thus not the only failing, but it did most to give the case its air of certainty. Expert evidence persuades in proportion to its apparent precision, and a figure of one in 73 million conveys an authority that the reasoning behind it may not deserve.

The case has become a standard warning, and the lessons drawn from it are of two kinds. The first concerns the competence of experts. A specialist in one field, however eminent, is not thereby a specialist in the statistics on which his testimony depends, and courts have since grown more cautious about unscrutinised figures. The second concerns the audience. Jurors are not, as a rule, trained to distinguish a probability from its converse, and good faith offers no protection against the fallacy. Some have urged that experts present statistical evidence in natural frequencies, saying that out of a thousand such families a certain number would be expected to experience each outcome, which most people reason about more accurately than they do about probabilities.

None of this is an argument against statistics in court; the right use of numbers would have shown that the case against Clark was far weaker than it seemed. It is an argument for asking, of any improbable event, whether the rival explanation is itself improbable. Rare events happen, and that something is unlikely is no evidence that it occurred by design unless the alternative is less so.
questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?

The chance that someone who has been struck by lightning was outdoors is very high; the chance that someone outdoors will be struck is very low.

To answer the right question one must compare explanations. Two babies dying naturally in one family is extremely rare; so is a mother murdering two of her children. Both explanations are improbable, and the evidence is that one of them occurred. The sensible question is therefore which is the less improbable, and that requires estimating the frequency of double murder as well as that of double cot death. When statisticians attempted this, they concluded that, on the figures available, a double natural death was at least as probable as a double murder, and perhaps considerably more so. The very rarity that appeared to condemn Clark applied equally to the case against her.

There was a further circumstance. Evidence of a bacterial infection in the second child, which might have supported a natural explanation, had not been disclosed to the defence by the pathologist, and its discovery was a ground for the second appeal. The statistical error was thus not the only failing, but it did most to give the case its air of certainty. Expert evidence persuades in proportion to its apparent precision, and a figure of one in 73 million conveys an authority that the reasoning behind it may not deserve.

The case has become a standard warning, and the lessons drawn from it are of two kinds. The first concerns the competence of experts. A specialist in one field, however eminent, is not thereby a specialist in the statistics on which his testimony depends, and courts have since grown more cautious about unscrutinised figures. The second concerns the audience. Jurors are not, as a rule, trained to distinguish a probability from its converse, and good faith offers no protection against the fallacy. Some have urged that experts present statistical evidence in natural frequencies, saying that out of a thousand such families a certain number would be expected to experience each outcome, which most people reason about more accurately than they do about probabilities.

None of this is an argument against statistics in court; the right use of numbers would have shown that the case against Clark was far weaker than it seemed. It is an argument for asking, of any improbable event, whether the rival explanation is itself improbable. Rare events happen, and that something is unlikely is no evidence that it occurred by design unless the alternative is less so.

Species such as the giant sequoia, whose cones open and whose seedlings thrive after fire, were failing to regenerate. The policy had removed a process on which the forests had come to depend.

For thousands of years lightning, and for much of that time the deliberate burning practised by Native peoples, had been part of how they worked, thinning stands, recycling nutrients and creating mosaics of habitat of different ages. The result is a fire hotter and harder to stop than those of the past. A policy designed to avoid disaster had, in effect, stored it.

Interviewer: Why do prices end in .99? Surely nobody is fooled.

Economist: Surprisingly, many are, though perhaps fewer than you would think. The leading explanation is the left-digit effect: we read from the left, so 3.99 registers as three-something and not as four. Field experiments with catalogues found that raising a price from 34 to 39 dollars increased sales, which is absurd if shoppers were reasoning about value. But it is not the whole story. Prices ending in nine also signal a sale, and retailers who use them to mark discounts train shoppers to treat them as discounts.

Interviewer: So it is a trick?

Economist: It is a trick that works only while shoppers do not think hard. When the stakes rise, say a car or a house, the effect weakens, because people deliberate. That is the pattern I would expect from a bias in fast, automatic judgement, and not from a mistake in values.

3. In practice, people often continue a failing project because of the effort already invested in it.
4. A sunk cost is a cost that has already been incurred and cannot be recovered.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The sentences build in this order: (4) A sunk cost... then (1) Rational decisions... then (3) In practice, people... then (2) The tendency explains.... Answer: 4132.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Other bees, following the dancer in the dark, can fly directly to the source without having seen it.
2. In addition, the duration of the waggling run indicates how far away the food lies.
3. Honeybees communicate the location of food by means of a dance performed on the wall of the hive.
4. The angle of the dance relative to the vertical corresponds to the direction of the food relative to the sun.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The sentences build in this order: (3) Honeybees communicate... then (4) The angle of the dance... then (2) In addition, the duration... then (1) Other bees, following.... Answer: 3421.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Periods of high unemployment can leave lasting effects. Workers who lose jobs in a recession lose skills and contacts, and employers treat long spells without work as a signal of low quality. The result is that, when demand recovers, many of the long-term unemployed do not return to work, and the economy settles at a higher rate of unemployment than before. The effect is called hysteresis, and it implies that temporary downturns can have permanent costs.'
options: A) Unemployment returns to its earlier level soon after demand recovers, since workers keep their skills throughout a recession.
B) Employers prefer to hire the long-term unemployed, because they have more time in which to learn the skills that the job requires.
C) Hysteresis: lost skills and a bad signal mean recessions can permanently raise unemployment.
D) Recessions are caused by hysteresis, which arises when workers lose their skills and employers stop hiring new people.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph describes how recessions leave lasting damage through lost skills and employer signalling. B, C and D reverse or confuse the cause and effect.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Pompeii is often called a frozen moment, a Roman city caught in a single afternoon. The image misleads. The city had been damaged by an earthquake some seventeen years earlier and was in the middle of repairs when Vesuvius erupted; many buildings were scaffolded and some houses stood empty. Nor did the ash preserve everything: fragile and organic things decayed, and looters and later excavators removed much. What we see is a city in the process of changing, through a selective record.'
options: A) Pompeii is not a frozen moment but a city under repair, selectively preserved and altered by digging.
B) Pompeii was destroyed by an earthquake and not by the eruption of Vesuvius, which came a good many years afterwards.
C) The preservation of Pompeii was complete, and everything that the city contained has been found by its excavators.
D) Pompeii had been abandoned by its inhabitants long before the eruption, and so tells us nothing about Roman life.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph corrects the 'frozen moment' image: repairs were under way, preservation was partial, and excavators removed things. The others contradict it.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'The traditional view in economics held that people choose so as to maximise their own welfare, and that consistent choices reveal preferences. Behavioural research has shown that choices are shaped by framing, defaults and mood, so that the same person may choose differently when the same options are described differently. If so, observed choices cannot be assumed to reveal welfare, and policy based on them may mistake the product of a quirk for the expression of a preference.'
options: A) People choose consistently in all circumstances, and behavioural research has confirmed the traditional economic view of choice.
B) Since choices vary with framing, they may not reveal preferences, which challenges welfare policy.
C) Policy should ignore the choices that people make, since they are always the product of mood and have nothing to do with welfare.
D) Framing and defaults affect only those people who have never received any education in economics or in statistics.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph contrasts the traditional view with behavioural findings and draws the implication for policy. The others reverse or overstate this.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'A rule that nobody can follow is worse than no rule. ________ Consider a regulation that requires a company to document every decision in a way that takes more time than the decisions themselves: the company will comply in form, and the paperwork will become a ritual unconnected with the care it was meant to ensure. The cost of excessive rules is not only the labour of obeying them but the decay of respect for rules in general.'
options: A) Regulation should therefore be abolished, since companies are always able to regulate themselves without any outside rules at all.
B) Companies that document every decision make better decisions than companies that do not keep such records of their work.
C) Respect for rules grows in proportion to their number and to the labour that is needed in order to obey them.
D) Rules that demand more than people can deliver breed formal compliance in place of the conduct the rules were meant to secure.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The sentences that follow show formal compliance replacing real care. B, C and D contradict or distort this.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'Many stories about inventions credit a single genius. ________ The telephone, the light bulb and the calculus were each announced by more than one person within a short span, which suggests that the conditions for them had matured and that the discovery was waiting to be made. The individual who happens to be first is celebrated, but the circumstances would probably have produced another.'
options: A) Inventors are rarely talented, and their success is a matter of luck alone, whatever the field in which they work.
B) Credit for an invention should always be shared equally among all those who have worked in the same field of study.
C) In fact, important inventions are often made independently by several people at about the same time.
D) No invention has ever been made by a single person working without any knowledge of the work of others.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'However' sets up the contrast with the single-genius stories, which the examples then support. B, C and D overstate or distort.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'Silence in conversation is usually felt as a failure. ________ In some cultures a pause before replying is a sign of respect and thought, and an interlocutor who answers at once may seem to have given the question too little weight. Where such norms meet others that prize quick replies, each side tends to misread the other: the one finds its partner impatient and shallow, the other finds it cold or evasive.'
options: A) Pauses always mean that a speaker has nothing to say, whatever the culture in which the conversation takes place.
B) Yet the meaning of a pause is not universal, and varies from one culture to another.
C) Quick replies are always a sign of respect, since they show that the speaker has thought carefully about the question.
D) Silence should be avoided in any conversation between members of different cultures, as it will only cause offence.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Yet' signals a contrast with the usual view; the examples then show how meanings differ across cultures. The others contradict the paragraph.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence:

The scholar's ________ prose, thick with qualification and jargon, defeated all but the most determined readers.
options: A) turgid
B) transparent
C) succinct
D) lucid
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Turgid' means swollen and tediously pompous. 'Transparent', 'succinct' and 'lucid' describe clear, economical writing.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence:

The treaty was ________ to the interests of the smaller states, which were given no voice in its drafting.
options: A) conducive
B) beneficial
C) congenial
D) inimical
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Inimical' means harmful or hostile. The other options suggest that the treaty helped the smaller states.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence:

The argument was dismissed as circular, since ________.
options: A) it had been put forward by a scholar who was not a recognised authority on the question
B) it relied upon figures that had been collected a great many years before the debate took place
C) its conclusion was assumed in one of its premises
D) it was so lengthy and complicated that few of those who heard it could follow its steps
questions.explanation: Explanation: A circular argument assumes what it sets out to prove. Only the first option states that. The others criticise the arguer, the data or the length.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best fills the blanks:

Though her manner was ________, her criticism was ________, and the author, ________ at the absence of the praise he had expected, left the room in silence.
options: A) gracious; withering; exhilarated
B) belligerent; withering; deflated
C) gracious; undemanding; deflated
D) gracious; withering; deflated
questions.explanation: Explanation: A gracious manner contrasts ('though') with withering criticism, which deflated the author. 'Exhilarated' contradicts the absence of praise; 'belligerent' and 'undemanding' break the contrast set up by 'though'.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best fills the blanks:

A ________ observer might have thought the dispute trivial, but to those involved it was a matter of ________ principle, which they were unwilling to ________.
options: A) calm; fundamental; compromise
B) partisan; fundamental; compromise
C) calm; trivial; compromise
D) calm; fundamental; endorse
questions.explanation: Explanation: A calm observer might think it trivial, but to the parties it was fundamental, and they would not compromise. 'Partisan' would not see it as trivial; 'trivial' contradicts 'but'; 'endorse' does not fit 'unwilling'.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: A) The proposal gained the assent of all the directors after a short discussion of the terms.
B) The reporters waited with baited breath for the verdict to be announced.
C) Her curiosity was piqued by the unusual title of the book that she had found on the shelf.
D) The climbers began their ascent at dawn, hoping to reach the summit of the mountain by noon.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The idiom is 'with bated breath' (held in suspense); 'baited' means furnished with bait. 'Assent' (agreement), 'piqued' (aroused) and 'ascent' (climb) are used correctly.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: A) The storm wreaked havoc on the coastal villages, destroying hundreds of homes in a single night.
B) The government gave the tenants a notice to quit the building within a month of the order.
C) She sought to home her skills as a negotiator by attending a series of workshops.
D) He decided to cite two recent studies in support of his argument at the meeting of the board.
questions.explanation: Explanation: To improve a skill is to 'hone' it; 'home' is a place. 'Wreaked' (inflicted), 'tenants' and 'cite' (quote) are used correctly.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'OSTENTATIOUS':
options: A) Showy
B) Modest
C) Reticent
D) Inconspicuous
questions.explanation: Explanation: Ostentatious means designed to impress; 'showy' is closest. 'Modest' and 'inconspicuous' are opposites.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'ALACRITY':
options: A) Eagerness
B) Torpor
C) Promptness
D) Briskness
questions.explanation: Explanation: Alacrity is cheerful readiness; 'torpor' (sluggish inactivity) is the antonym. The others are synonyms.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'INCHOATE':
options: A) Complete
B) Elaborate
C) Fastidious
D) Nascent
questions.explanation: Explanation: Inchoate means just begun and not fully formed; 'nascent' is closest. 'Complete' is the opposite.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'VERBOSE':
options: A) Wordy
B) Prolix
C) Concise
D) Long-winded
questions.explanation: Explanation: Verbose means using more words than needed; 'concise' is the antonym. The others are synonyms.

questions.question:
Choose the correct meaning of the idiom:
'To beat around the bush' means to:
options: A) search carefully for something that has been lost in a place with many hiding spots
B) avoid coming to the point
C) attack a weaker opponent who has no means of defending himself against the blows
D) make a great deal of noise in order to frighten away the animals that live nearby
questions.explanation: Explanation: To beat around the bush is to talk without getting to the main point.

questions.question: Select the sentence in which 'ALLUDE' is used correctly:
options: A) In his speech, the minister alluded to the scandal without naming anyone.
B) The soldiers managed to allude capture for three weeks in the mountains.
C) She alluded the question by changing the subject at the first opportunity.
D) The magician's skill allowed him to allude the attention of the whole audience.
questions.explanation: Explanation: To 'allude' is to refer indirectly. The other sentences need 'elude' (evade).

questions.question:
Choose the best replacement for the underlined portion:

Having been warned by the guide, <u>the stream was crossed by the travellers</u> with great care.
options: A) crossing the stream was done by the travellers
B) the crossing of the stream was made by the travellers
C) the stream, by the travellers, was crossed
D) the travellers crossed the stream
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Having been warned' must modify the people who were warned, so 'the travellers' must be the subject: 'the travellers crossed the stream'. In the other options the subject is something else, leaving the modifier dangling.

questions.question:
Choose the best replacement for the underlined portion:

She is <u>more intelligent than any student</u> in her class.
options: A) more intelligent than all of the students
B) most intelligent than any student
C) more intelligent than any other student
D) the more intelligent than any student
questions.explanation: Explanation: Comparing a member of a group with the rest of the group requires 'other': 'more intelligent than any other student'.

questions.question:
Spot the error in the following sentence:
'The committee has (A) / discussed the matter (B) / at length, and (C) / they has agreed (D).'
options: A) The committee has
B) discussed the matter
C) at length, and
D) they has agreed
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'They' takes 'have', not 'has': 'they have agreed'.

questions.question:
Spot the error in the following sentence:
'Between you and I (A) / the plan put forward is (B) / unlikely to be accepted (C) / by the whole committee (D).'
options: A) Between you and I
B) the plan put forward is
C) unlikely to be accepted
D) by the whole committee
questions.explanation: Explanation: After a preposition the object pronoun is used: 'between you and me'.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
options: A) The number of applications have risen sharply this year.
B) The number of applications has risen sharply this year.
C) A number of applications has risen sharply this year.
D) The numbers of applications is rising sharply this year.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'The number of' takes a singular verb: 'has risen'. 'A number of' takes a plural verb.

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'She suggested that he ________ a doctor.'
options: A) see
B) sees
C) saw
D) has seen
questions.explanation: Explanation: After verbs of suggestion the subjunctive (base form) is used: 'suggested that he see'.

questions.question: Identify the grammatically INCORRECT sentence:
options: A) Each of the boys has finished his work before the time was called.
B) If it rains in the afternoon, we shall stay at home and read.
C) Having finished the exam, the bell rang.
D) She has lived in Delhi since 2015, and she intends to stay on.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Having finished the exam' must modify the person who finished it, not 'the bell'; the modifier dangles. The other sentences are correct.

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'He is accused ________ breach of trust.'
options: A) for
B) of
C) with
D) on
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Accused' takes 'of'.
